newsitem.title: USA: Canada's Chretien in Washington for Clinton talks.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien in Washington for Clinton talks.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on Monday began his first official visit to the United States during which he will hold wide-ranging talks with President Bill Clinton.

Chretien will have 70 minutes of talks with Clinton on Tuesday, the Canadian embassy said, and White House officials said Clinton had invited the Canadian for coffee in his family quarters at the White House on Monday night.
The officials said there would be no media coverage of the coffee, which was to take place at 9 p.m. EST (0100 GMT on Tuesday). The leaders' wives will not attend.

On Tuesday Clinton will hold a series of meetings with Chretien at the White House, beginning with a morning arrival ceremony on the South Lawn, a meeting in the Oval Office and an early afternoon joint news conference in the Rose Garden.
The two leaders will discuss bilateral ties including a dispute over a U.S. law, opposed by Canada, that would punish some foreign firms that do business with communist-ruled Cuba.
Clinton and Chretien will also discuss cross-border environmental issues and enhancing the world's richest bilateral trade relationship, valued at $1 billion a day, diplomats said.
Clinton will host a dinner for Chretien in the evening. Formally, this will not be a "state dinner" because Chretien is not Canada's head of state.

Chretien on Monday met with World Bank President James Wolfensohn and discussed the Bank's plan for reorganization and how the Bank and Canada can work together to help improve conditions in Africa, officials said.

As part of that, they discussed an upcoming global knowledge conference in Toronto in June at which the use of technology to assist developing countries to improve education -- called distance learning -- will be explored.
Chretien's delegation included environmental officials who met with their American counterparts and agreed to coordinate efforts for getting rid of toxic chemicals from the Great Lakes.

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner and Canadian Minister of the Environment Sergio Marchi also agreed to work together to find out how big a problem cross-border smog is and coordinate environmental research.
